notes:
I couldn't find real tradition-by-tradition disagreement for 1 Kings 1:1–26. Commentators do disagree, mainly about whether Abishag was David's concubine, but they split as individuals rather than along denominational lines. I found nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. Pentecostal-specific views also turned up nothing beyond Guzik's Enduring Word page.

**v. 1**
- David was about 70. Guzik says this was the end of a great reign, and that David was too weak even to keep warm, let alone rule. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- The Pulpit Commentary works out from 2 Samuel 5:4–5 that David could not have been over seventy. It suggests early hardship and later sorrow aged him early, and he may also have been ill. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/1.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch say this small detail is recorded for two reasons: it shows David was too weak to govern, and Adonijah later lost his life by asking to marry Abishag. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-1.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik calls this a recognised medical treatment of the time, mentioned by the Greek doctor Galen. Josephus even calls the "servants" physicians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- The Pulpit Commentary explains the details. She had to be young to give off warmth, and a virgin as suited a king. Though put forward as a nurse, people would naturally assume she might become a concubine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/1.htm

**v. 3**
- Shunem was a town in Issachar near the Little Hermon hill (today's Solam). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/1-kings-1.html
- Some have linked Abishag with the "Shulammite" of the Song of Solomon. Guzik, quoting Wiseman, says this is guesswork at best: Shunem and Shulam are different places. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/

**v. 4** *(the main point of disagreement)*
- **Concubine or secondary wife:**
  - Matthew Henry held that Abishag was married to David as a secondary wife. His evidence is that Adonijah's later wish to marry her was treated as a serious crime. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_001.cfm
  - Guzik says David almost certainly made her his concubine. Taking more than one wife was unwise but not then forbidden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
  - The Lutheran Kretzmann says her relationship to David was seen as that of a wife. The note that "the king knew her not" explains how Adonijah could later ask for her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-kings-1.html
- **Simply an attendant:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary disagrees. It says the idea of a legal marriage has no support in Scripture, which presents her only as an attendant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/1.htm
  - The Gospel Coalition commentary says she never officially joined the harem. She was an appointed caregiver, though Solomon treated that as the same thing, and her limited role shows David could no longer rule. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-kings/
- **Middle positions:**
  - Whedon calls the argument needless. Sleeping beside the king put her more or less in a concubine's position, which is why Solomon read Adonijah's request as a claim to the throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/1-kings-1.html
  - A GotQuestions article (quoted on Precept Austin) agrees there was no sexual relationship, but says people assumed she was in effect part of the harem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-1-commentary
- **Catholic/Orthodox (Church Father):**
  - Jerome, in his Letter 52, calls the passage "mystical teaching." He reads Abishag as the wisdom that grows warmer as the body ages. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001052.htm
  - Schaff explains that Jerome thought a literal reading was absurd, since David still had wives living. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/hcc3/hcc3.iii.xiii.xvii.html

**v. 5**
- Adonijah was the fourth son and probably the oldest still living. By custom he looked like the heir, but God chose Israel's king. Guzik says he broke the principle that we let God lift us up rather than raising ourselves. The chariots and runners copy Absalom (2 Samuel 15:1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- The Pulpit Commentary says Israel had no automatic right of the firstborn, though seniority still counted. It lists his likely motives: his age, his good looks, encouragement from Joab, and possibly his desire for Abishag. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/1.htm
- Precept Austin says Adonijah and Absalom both tried to be king against God's will, and both died. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-1-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik says David did poorly at disciplining his sons. He suggests David may have had a poor example from his own father, but says that is no excuse. He quotes Trapp: David was always "too fond a father." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- Matthew Henry warns that spoiled children learn pride and ambition. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_001.cfm
- Kretzmann calls this another sign of David's weakness toward his children. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-kings-1.html

**v. 7**
- Joab may have resented being passed over for Amasa. Abiathar may have been jealous of Zadok. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests Joab feared losing his place under Solomon. It thinks Adonijah may have promised Abiathar's family sole control of the priesthood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/1.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch reject the idea that Joab backed Adonijah because Adonijah was in the right. Joab never cared much about right. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-1.html
- Ellicott suggests people may not have seen Adonijah's move as outright rebellion. Solomon was young, and David's choice of him could be written off as an old man's favouritism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/1.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: Zadok came from Eleazar's line and Abiathar from Ithamar's. Benaiah commanded the bodyguard. Ewald guessed Shimei and Rei were David's brothers, but they would have been very old by then. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/1.htm
- Gill reports a view that Rei was Hushai. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-8.html
- Precept Austin says this Shimei is not the one who cursed David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-1-commentary
- Constable thinks he might be, and may have been loyal or just looking out for himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-8.html

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary calls it a sacrificial feast like Absalom's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/1.htm
- Matthew Poole says the aim was to get God on his side and draw a crowd. Cambridge notes the Hebrew verb is the usual word for sacrificing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-9.htm
- Ellicott says the meaning of "Zoheleth" is uncertain (possibly "serpent's stone"). He calls En-rogel the "spring of the fuller," near Siloam. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/1-9.htm
- The Catholic Haydock commentary says the animals were either sacrificed or just used for a feast, though peace offerings were likely. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-9.html

**v. 10**
- Keil & Delitzsch say leaving Solomon out shows Adonijah knew Solomon had been chosen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-1.html
- The Ryrie Study Bible (quoted on Precept Austin) suggests he may have planned to kill them. Had they eaten with him, he would have been bound to protect them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-1-commentary

**v. 11**
- Barnes thinks "son of Haggith" was chosen to sting Bathsheba: the son of her rival. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-11.html
- Constable says Adonijah was "king" only as the crowd's choice for the moment. Nathan may have been trying to shock Bathsheba. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-5.html
- Guzik says the verse also shows how out of touch David was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/

**v. 12**
- If Adonijah won, all rivals would have been killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-11.html
- Guzik agrees: Adonijah would have killed Bathsheba and Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/

**v. 13**
- The traditional reading (Guzik) is that David's oath is not recorded earlier, but 1 Chronicles 22:5–9 confirms he meant Solomon to reign. Guzik sees grace in the son of David's worst scandal becoming heir. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- **Modern scholarship:** Sara Koenig (Bible Odyssey) notes that because the promise is never shown, some think Bathsheba made it up, and others that Nathan used her. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/en/people/main-articles/bathsheba.aspx
- Another Bible Odyssey article says Solomon won through "careful manipulation" of the aging David. https://blog.bibleodyssey.org/articles/solomon/

**v. 14**
- Nathan knew David went easy on his sons and would struggle to believe the news, so he arranged a convincing two-part report. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/

**v. 15**
- The note about Abishag reminds us how limited David was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- Pett observes that Abishag was allowed to stay at every audience. That would let her hear state secrets and makes her look like a royal wife. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-1.html

**v. 16**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the very old king, attended by Abishag, could not leave his room, so Bathsheba went in to him and bowed low. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-11.html

**vv. 17–18**
- Keil & Delitzsch say the repeated "and now" shows how forcefully Bathsheba spoke. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-kings-1.html

**v. 19**
- Pett says Adonijah was claiming a joint rule for himself. Leaving Solomon out was full of meaning, and David, who was not senile, would see it at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/1-kings-1.html

**vv. 20–21**
- Guzik calls this a tender appeal: Bathsheba's life and Solomon's were in danger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- Matthew Henry says that if Adonijah won, Solomon's friends would be treated as traitors, because usurpers are the cruellest rulers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_001.cfm

**vv. 22–23**
- Nathan, who had once rebuked David over Bathsheba, was still a trusted friend. Trapp says David loved him more for his honesty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- Ellicott says Nathan appears here more as a chief adviser than in his role as a prophet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/1.htm

**v. 24**
- The Gospel Coalition commentary hears disbelief in Nathan's question: if David had done this, he had broken faith with Nathan and Zadok. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-kings/

**v. 25**
- Kretzmann says the cry literally means "May King Adonijah live!" https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-kings-1.html

**v. 26**
- Kretzmann says every move Adonijah made showed hostility to the king's friends. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-kings-1.html
- Kelly calls Benaiah the true servant of the king's plans and Nathan the one who spoke God's mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-8.html
